title: The moon from behind a cloud (172–178)
word: The moon from behind a cloud
hook: one who was careless and becomes earnest lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bubble: look upon the world as a bubble, as a mirage. Your line was a bubble, a mirage. Did something heavy get lighter when you saw it that way? Day one hundred ninety-two.

You were doing so well. Three weeks of sitting every morning, and then a trip, a cold, a hard week, and suddenly it's been ten days. And now there's a small, heavy feeling whenever you think about starting again. Because starting again means admitting you stopped. Most people quit right there, not because they failed, but because beginning again feels embarrassing. Tonight, look up if you can. Even the moon disappears for a while, behind clouds, and nobody thinks less of it when it comes back. Today: the moon from behind a cloud.
screen: `THREE GOOD WEEKS, THEN TEN DAYS.` → `STARTING AGAIN FEELS EMBARRASSING.` → `EVEN THE MOON DISAPPEARS.`

segments.voice: Verse one seventy-two, in Max Müller's translation: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Reckless here means heedless, careless, the opposite of the earnestness from chapter two. Notice that the verse doesn't say the careless past vanishes. It says the person, now awake, gives light. Then verse one seventy-three goes further: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." And the old commentary attaches this verse to the most dramatic turnaround in the Buddha's story: Aṅgulimāla, the bandit who wore a garland of his victims' fingers, who met the Buddha, stopped, became a monk, and was remembered as having reached awakening. If the moon can come out from behind that cloud, the verse is saying, it can come out from behind yours. The Pali word for moon here is candimā, and the image is one every village knew: the full moon sliding free of a cloud, and suddenly you can see the whole road. The chapter ends with a striking claim, verse one seventy-eight: "Better than sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all worlds, is the reward of the first step in holiness." The first step: in the tradition, the moment one first truly enters the stream of the path. Not the finish line. The first step, and the second beginning, and the third.
screen: `RECKLESS, THEN SOBER.` · `DEEDS COVERED BY GOOD DEEDS.` · `AṄGULIMĀLA'S TURNAROUND.` · `THE FIRST STEP OUTSHINES EMPIRES.` · then, large: `THE MOON COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one practice you've let slip. Sitting, a precept, a kindness you used to do, exercise, a call you used to make. Notice the little cloud of embarrassment around it. You don't have to push it away. Just picture the moon behind a thin cloud, and the cloud slowly drifting on. Then begin again, right now, in the smallest way: this breath counts. This sit counts. Whatever you let slip, the moon is already coming out. The bell holds the time.
The moon from behind a cloud. Verse one seventy-two: one who was careless and then became earnest lights up the world, like the moon freed from clouds.
screen: `THE MOON FROM BEHIND A CLOUD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the moon comes out. Today, begin one lapsed thing again, without apology or ceremony, and if you see the moon tonight, let it remind you. Day one hundred ninety-two.

screen: `DAY 192 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HARD TO BE BORN HUMAN.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often point to Aṅgulimāla's story and these verses to encourage people to begin again after lapses, and lay Buddhists retake the precepts regularly as a fresh start.

match.prompt: match each piece of today's verses.

myth: the verse says the careless past simply vanishes
it says the person, now awake, brightens the world, like the moon freed from clouds.
the commentary links verse 173 to Aṅgulimāla
the bandit who became a monk is the verse's great example.
verse 178 prizes ruling the whole earth above the first step on the path
the reward of the first step is better than sovereignty over the earth.

fork.setup: you're Aṅgulimāla. you've done terrible harm, and now you've met the Buddha and stopped. what does verse 173 say is possible?
options: good deeds can cover the harm, and you can brighten the world.
forget the past and carry on as before.
fork.reveal: "he whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world." tradition remembers Aṅgulimāla reaching awakening.

original.note: Pali: the moon — in verses 172–173, the moon freed from a cloud.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty image about the moon.
what it means: anyone who was careless and turns earnest gives light, however heavy the clouds were.
what a scholar hears: the commentary ties verse 173 to Aṅgulimāla, and verse 178's 'first step in holiness' is sotāpatti, entering the stream.
